query: Starting from a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, what single intervention could overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated starting catalyst, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A post‐synthesis controlled acid‐etching treatment, optionally combined with a low‐temperature nitrogen anneal, will generate a Px‐enriched, ultra‐thin protective shell on the nearly equiatomic multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst that overcomes activity losses and durability challenges under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst with nearly equiatomic concentrations of several principal elements, including a low fraction of platinum-group metals, in a homogeneous solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Apply a precise post‐synthesis acid‐etching treatment followed by a low‐temperature nitrogen anneal to selectively leach less noble metals and incorporate nitrogen, thereby promoting platinum segregation at the surface.
generation.conditions: Simulated transient and low‐temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust environments containing controlled levels of H2O and NO, combined with thermal cycling protocols that emulate long-term mileage.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a core–shell structure in which an intact high-entropy alloy core is protected by a nanoscale, Pt-rich shell fortified by metal–nitrogen bonds.
generation.mechanism: Acidic dealloying selectively removes less stable metals, driving platinum to segregate toward the surface; subsequently, nitrogen incorporation reinforces the shell via M–N bonding. This dual modification optimizes the electronic structure and protects against sintering, oxidation, and poisoning by exhaust constituents.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated catalyst is expected to exhibit improved catalytic activity retention and enhanced durability relative to the untreated catalyst under simulated automotive exhaust conditions, while using a reduced overall amount of platinum. The magnitude of improvement is uncertain and will depend on the precise optimization of treatment parameters.
generation.baseline: The untreated multi‐element alloy catalyst degrades over time under transient, low‐temperature exhaust conditions due to structural dealloying, sintering, and poisoning by H2O and NO.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected when the treatment parameters (acid concentration, etching duration, nitrogen annealing temperature) are finely tuned; extreme deviations from these parameters or operating conditions far outside typical automotive exhaust environments may not yield the same performance benefits.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by structural and catalytic performance studies, the exact quantitative improvement in activity retention and durability under real-world conditions remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the multi‐element alloy catalyst from an identical synthesis route. Subject one batch to the controlled acid-etching plus low-temperature nitrogen anneal treatment, while using the other batch as an untreated control. Expose both batches to simulated transient, low‐temperature exhaust conditions with controlled H2O and NO content along with thermal cycling that mimics increased mileage.
measurements: Catalytic performance metrics (e.g., conversion rates of exhaust model compounds such as CO, NO, or hydrocarbons) measured over time
Surface composition and structural characterization (via XPS, TEM, and elemental mapping) to verify the formation and uniformity of the Pt-rich and nitrogen-incorporated shell
Durability assessment through accelerated aging tests quantifying activity retention and platinum dissolution rates (e.g., via ICP-MS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated catalyst does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in catalytic activity retention and durability—as evidenced by similar or greater Pt loss, no clear formation of a Pt-rich/nitrogen-doped shell, or no reduction in deactivation rates compared to the untreated control—then the hypothesis is falsified.

The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst possesses a unique structure and electrochemical stability, resulting in excellent long-term durability under HDV conditions. Detailed studies on atomic structure utilizing in situ synchrotron XRD and XAS, coupled with HAADF-STEM/EDS and DFT calculations, allowed the elucidation of influencing factors on the catalytic properties and performance of the novel catalyst. The high performance of N–Pt/HEA/C originates from the combined effect of high entropy, multiple M-N bonds, and a Pt-rich shell. In addition to the enhancement of corrosion resistance, the M–N bonds through N-doping can boost the activity and durability of the electrocatalyst by the distortion effect in the core structure. The synergy between the three factors further endows the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst to outperform the state-of-the-art Pt/C electrocatalysts and most binary/ternary Pt-based catalysts for the ORR. AbstractThe stability of a nanoparticle catalyst during electrochemical reaction is crucial for its application. Despite increasing interest in multi-metallic alloy nanoparticles, such as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), for electrocatalysis and emerging models for their catalytic activity, there is limited work on frameworks that can predict the metastability of these alloys under reaction conditions, including stability against electrochemical surface dissolution. Incorporating electrochemical stability in multi-objective optimization would advance HEAs as a catalyst discovery platform. To address the knowledge gap on electrochemical stability, we propose a methodology for simulating the dissolution of n-element alloy nanoparticles comprised of density functional theory and machine-learning regression to calculate the dissolution potentials of the surface atoms. We demonstrate the methodology for the Ag–Au–Cu–Ir–Pd–Pt–Rh–Ru HEA system with the conditions of the oxygen reduction reaction. drafts.hypothesis: A controlled, moderate‐temperature oxidative pre‐treatment in an exhaust‐simulating atmosphere (containing H2O and NO) applied to the multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst will induce selective surface segregation and formation of a nanoscale protective oxide overlayer. This intervention is expected to stabilize the active sites and suppress sintering or degradation during thermal aging, thereby overcoming activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal usage.
drafts.material_initial_state: Multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst with nearly equiatomic ratios of several principal elements, including minor platinum-group-metal content, in an as-synthesized state.
drafts.intervention: A single controlled oxidative pre-treatment by heating the catalyst at moderate temperature in an atmosphere containing controlled levels of H2O and NO (and likely a small oxygen fraction) before exposure to actual exhaust conditions.
drafts.conditions: Pretreatment performed under conditions that mimic low‐temperature, transient exhaust environments; subsequent catalytic testing under simulated gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust conditions with H2O, NO, and thermal aging cycles.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a nanoscale, protective oxide overlayer via selective segregation of one or more alloy constituents (e.g., reactive elements already present) to the surface.
drafts.mechanism: The oxidative pre-treatment initiates surface reconstruction that enriches the catalyst surface with stabilized oxide clusters. These clusters act as barriers against further sintering or coarsening during thermal cycling and protect active sites from deleterious reactions with H2O and NO, thereby maintaining catalytic activity and durability over prolonged use.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Treated catalysts will show improved retention of catalytic activity and enhanced durability relative to untreated catalysts after simulated thermal aging and mileage, with less Pt loss or sintering, under conditions representative of transient and low-temperature exhaust operation.
drafts.baseline: Performance of the untreated multi-element alloy catalyst under identical transient, low-temperature, and aging conditions where notable activity loss and durability issues are observed.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the catalyst possesses elements capable of surface segregation into stable oxides and when the pre-treatment conditions (temperature, gas composition, and duration) are optimized to favor the formation of a coherent protective overlayer without significant loss of active sites. It may not hold if the alloy lacks sufficiently reactive elements or if pre-treatment conditions are too aggressive.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts from the same multi-element alloy batch. Apply the oxidative pre-treatment (moderate temperature in H2O/NO atmosphere) to one set while leaving the other untreated. Subject both sets to simulated transient/exhaust conditions including low-temperature operation and controlled thermal aging cycles. Compare the catalytic activity (e.g., conversion rates of relevant exhaust components) and physical characteristics (e.g., particle sintering via microscopy) before and after aging.
measurements: Structural analysis (TEM/SEM of particle size and oxide layer formation)
Surface composition (XPS to detect surface segregation and oxide species)
Durability metrics (activity retention over time and thermal cycles)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated catalysts do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in activity retention and durability (or if they degrade more significantly) compared to the untreated baseline under identical test conditions, or if no detectable protective oxide overlayer is formed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that induces in-situ formation of a protective, catalytically active mixed-metal oxide layer on the multi-element, nearly equiatomic alloy can overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption.
drafts.material_initial_state: Multi-element automotive alloy catalyst with multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, initially lacking a deliberate surface oxide layer.
drafts.intervention: Apply a post-synthetic, controlled oxidative treatment (pre-oxidation) to the catalyst to generate a thin, conformal mixed-metal oxide surface layer.
drafts.conditions: Test under transient and low‐temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust conditions including the presence of H2O and NO, followed by standard thermal aging and mileage-simulated cycling.
drafts.structural_mediator: A thin, robust mixed-metal oxide layer (formed in situ from selected elements in the alloy) that protects active sites and promotes enhanced redox cycling.
drafts.mechanism: The formation of the oxide layer stabilizes the surface structure against thermal degradation and poisoning (e.g., water and NO exposure) while preserving or even boosting catalytic activity. This layer facilitates oxygen storage and effective redox reactions, thus mitigating activity loss and durability issues without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The treated catalyst will exhibit superior catalytic activity (especially in low-temperature and transient conditions) and enhanced durability during extended thermal aging and mileage cycling compared to the untreated catalyst.
drafts.baseline: Performance metrics (activity, conversion rates, and durability) of the untreated multi-element alloy catalyst under identical operating and aging conditions.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under typical automotive exhaust conditions with transient low-temperature operations and standard thermal aging protocols; extreme conditions far outside these parameters may not see the same benefit.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the multi-element alloy catalyst: one receiving the controlled pre-oxidation treatment and one serving as the untreated control. Both batches will then be subjected to simulated transient and low-temperature exhaust conditions (including H2O and NO exposure) and accelerated thermal aging. Measure catalytic activity, conversion rates, and durability (e.g., performance degradation over mileage cycles).
measurements: Catalytic conversion efficiency at low temperatures
Surface characterization (e.g., XPS or TEM to confirm oxide layer formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated catalyst does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in catalytic performance and durability compared to the untreated catalyst, or if the protective oxide layer does not form as expected, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A well‐controlled post‐synthesis dealloying treatment that selectively leaches less‐noble elements will form an ultrathin, nitrogen‐stabilized Pt‐rich surface layer on the multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst. This core–shell modification is expected to mitigate activity loss and durability issues under transient, low‐temperature exhaust conditions while keeping overall platinum-group-metal usage low.
drafts.material_initial_state: An equiatomic multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst composed of several transition metals (including a low but essential fraction of platinum-group metals) in nearly uniform concentrations.
drafts.intervention: Apply a precisely controlled acid‐etching (and optional nitrogen doping) dealloying process to selectively remove more labile components from the surface, thereby creating a robust Pt‐rich shell over the original high‐entropy alloy core.
drafts.conditions: Transient and low‐temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust environments, with exposure to H2O and NO and under thermal aging (simulated increased mileage) conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: A core–shell architecture in which the high-entropy alloy core remains intact while a thin, chemically stable Pt‐rich shell (potentially reinforced by incorporated N forming strong M–N bonds) mediates the reaction at the surface.
drafts.mechanism: The newly formed Pt-rich surface offers enhanced catalytic active sites with optimal electronic properties that promote effective reactant adsorption and resistance against poisoning by water and nitric oxide. Simultaneously, the core–shell structure limits further dissolution or sintering during thermal cycling, and N-incorporation may further stabilize the bonding environment via multiple M–N interactions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under exhaust conditions, the dealloyed, core–shell catalyst should exhibit slower activity degradation, improved resistance to thermal and chemical stresses, and maintain comparable or higher catalytic performance relative to the untreated catalyst—while using less total platinum.
drafts.baseline: The untreated, nearly equiatomic multi‐element alloy catalyst suffers from activity loss and durability limitations under transient low-temperature exhaust conditions, with typical degradation arising from thermal aging, water/NO exposure, and component dissolution.
drafts.boundary: The improved performance is expected when the dealloying process is optimized to form a continuous and ultrathin Pt‐rich shell under laboratory-simulated transient operating temperatures (roughly 50–150 °C) and controlled aging protocols; effects may vary if the acid-etching parameters or N-doping level deviate from optimal ranges.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct accelerated aging tests comparing the original untreated catalyst and the dealloyed (and optionally N-doped) Pt-rich shell catalyst under simulated transient low-temperature exhaust conditions containing controlled levels of H2O and NO. Use thermal cycling and extended operation to simulate increased mileage.
measurements: Catalytic performance metrics (e.g., conversion rates of model exhaust components such as CO or NO)
Surface composition and structure (via XPS and TEM to verify Pt enrichment and nitrogen incorporation)
Pt dissolution rate (using ICP-MS analysis over cycling)
Activity retention after thermal aging cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post‐treatment catalyst does not show a statistically significant improvement in catalytic activity retention, durability (e.g., lower Pt dissolution and less activity drop over time), and stable Pt-rich surface formation compared to the untreated catalyst under identical test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A controlled post‐synthesis surface treatment—specifically, a mild acid-etching step followed by a low-temperature nitrogen anneal—will induce selective dealloying that causes platinum to segregate to the surface, creating a thin, Pt-rich shell fortified by metal–nitrogen bonds. This engineered surface reconstruction is expected to overcome activity loss and durability challenges under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions while keeping overall platinum use low.
drafts.material_initial_state: A multi-element high-entropy automotive catalyst with nearly equiatomic ratios of both noble (e.g., Pt) and base metals, presenting a homogeneous solid solution serving as the starting alloy.
drafts.intervention: Subject the as-synthesized catalyst to a controlled acid etching (to preferentially remove less noble metals from the surface) followed by a mild nitrogen atmosphere annealing to incorporate N into the surface structure.
drafts.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions including transient and low-temperature operation (typical of gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust), exposure to H2O and NO, along with thermal cycling that mimics long-term aging/mileage.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a nanoscale, protective Pt-rich shell enriched with metal–nitrogen (M–N) bonds, which acts both as a barrier against dealloying and as an electronic modifier of the active sites.
drafts.mechanism: The acid treatment selectively leaches out less noble elements at the alloy surface, promoting platinum segregation, while subsequent N-doping yields robust M–N bonds. This composite effect stabilizes the surface against oxidation, poisoning (by NO and moisture), and structural degradation under thermal cycling, and also modulates the electronic properties for optimal adsorption of reaction intermediates.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated catalyst, the treated catalyst will exhibit higher catalytic activity and significantly improved durability under harsh and cycling automotive exhaust conditions with minimal platinum loading, maintaining stable performance over extended operation.
drafts.baseline: Untreated multi-element HEA catalysts typically suffer from gradual activity loss and durability issues (e.g., dealloying, oxidation, and increased surface poisoning) when exposed to transient, low-temperature, wet, and NO-containing exhaust environments.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only when the acid etching and N annealing are properly optimized to form a uniform Pt-rich shell without over-etching, and may not be applicable to alloy systems with substantially different compositions or under extreme conditions beyond typical automotive exhaust ranges.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the starting HEA catalyst. Apply the acid-etching plus nitrogen annealing treatment to one batch while leaving the other untreated as a control. Then, expose both batches to simulated transient, low-temperature automotive exhaust conditions including programmed exposures to H2O and NO and repeated thermal cycling to mimic increased mileage. Structural characterization (TEM, XPS) and catalytic performance tests (activity measurements for pollutant conversion, durability testing over time) should be conducted before and after aging.
measurements: Catalytic activity (e.g., conversion rates of NO or CO) as a function of operating time
Surface composition and Pt segregation via XPS and TEM
Resistance to poisoning (e.g., changes in activity in the presence of NO/H2O)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated catalyst does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least 10% higher sustained activity and slower degradation rates) compared to the untreated catalyst over the simulated aging tests, or if surface analysis does not confirm the formation of a uniform Pt-rich/nitrogen-doped shell, then the hypothesis is falsified.
